# completeness {.divider}

The axiom system is *sound* and *complete* for the semantics of propositional logic.

::: {.theorem}
For each set of formulas $\Gamma$ and each formula $\varphi$, 
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \vdash \varphi & \Leftrightarrow & \Gamma \models \varphi\\
\end{array}
$$
:::


# soundness {.smaller}

The axiom system is *sound* if a formula $\varphi$ is derivable from a $\Gamma$ *only if* $\varphi$ is a logical consequence of $\Gamma$.

::: {.theorem}
**Soundness** For each set of formulas $\Gamma$ and each formula $\varphi$, 
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \vdash \varphi & \Rightarrow & \Gamma \models \varphi\\
\end{array}
$$
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.proof}
Use a *complete induction* on the *length* of derivations. Set the condition $\Phi(n)$ on *length* as: 

::: {style="border-left: 4px solid #2980b9; padding-left: 0.8em; margin: 0.8em 0; color: #2c3e50; font-weight: 500;"}
For each set of formulas $\Gamma$ and each formula $\varphi$, if $\langle \chi_1, \cdots \chi_n\rangle$ is a derivation of $\varphi$ from $\Gamma$ of length $n$, then $\Gamma \models \varphi$.
:::

:::

:::

# completeness {.smaller}

The axiom system is *complete* if if a formula $\varphi$ is derivable from a $\Gamma$ *whenever* $\varphi$ is a logical consequence of $\Gamma$.

::: {.theorem}
**Completeness** For each set of formulas $\Gamma$ and each formula $\varphi$, 
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \models \varphi & \Rightarrow & \Gamma \vdash \varphi\\
\end{array}
$$
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

We will set out to prove a reformulation of completeness in terms of *consistency*, a proof-theoretic counterpart of satisfiability.

::: {style="border: 2px solid #7f8c8d; background: #f8f9fa; padding: 0.5em 1em; border-radius: 6px; margin-top: 1.2em;"}
For each set of formulas $\Gamma$ and each formula $\varphi$, 

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \nvdash \varphi & \Rightarrow &\Gamma \not \models \varphi\\
\Gamma \models \varphi & \Rightarrow & \Gamma \vdash \varphi \\
\Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \textsf{consistent} & \Rightarrow & \Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \textsf{satisfiable} \\
\end{array}
$$

For each set of formulas $\Gamma$,

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma  \ \textsf{consistent} & \Rightarrow & \Gamma \ \textsf{satisfiable} \\
\end{array}
$$
:::

:::


## consistency

::: {.definition}
A set of formulas $\Gamma$ is *consistent* iff $\bot$ is not derivable from $\Gamma$.
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.theorem}
Given a set of formulas $\Gamma$ and a formula $\varphi$,
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \vdash \varphi &  \Leftrightarrow & \Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \ \text{is inconsistent}.\\
\end{array}
$$
:::
*Consistency* is the proof-theoretic counterpart of *satisfiability*:

::: {.theorem}
Given a set of formulas $\Gamma$ and a formula $\varphi$,
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \models \varphi &  \Leftrightarrow & \Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \ \text{is unsatisfiable}.\\
\end{array}
$$
:::

:::

## from left to right {.smaller}

::: {.theorem}
Given a set of formulas $\Gamma$ and a formula $\varphi$,
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \vdash \varphi &  \Rightarrow & \Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \ \text{is inconsistent}.\\
\end{array}
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Assume $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$. Here is a derivation of $\bot$ from $\Gamma, \neg \varphi$:

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
1 & & \neg \varphi \to (\neg \bot \to \neg  \varphi) & \textsf{A1}[\neg \varphi/p, \bot/q]  \\
2 & & \neg \varphi & \textsf{premise} \\
3 & & \neg \bot \to \neg \varphi & \textsf{MP} \ 1, 2\\
4 & & (\neg \bot \to \neg \varphi) \to (\varphi \to \bot) & \textsf{theorem} \ (4.3)\\
5 & & \varphi \to \bot & \textsf{MP} \ 3, 4\\
6 & & \varphi  & \Gamma \vdash \varphi\\
7 & & \bot & \textsf{MP} \ 4, 5\\
\end{array}
$$

:::

## from right to left {.smaller}

::: {.theorem}
Given a set of formulas $\Gamma$ and a formula $\varphi$,
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \ \text{is inconsistent} &  \Rightarrow & \Gamma \vdash \varphi\\
\end{array}
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Assume $\Gamma, \neg \varphi$ is inconsistent, i.e., $\Gamma, \neg \varphi \vdash \bot$. Here is a derivation of $\varphi$ from $\Gamma$:

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
1 & & \neg \varphi \to  \neg \bot & \Gamma \vdash \neg \varphi \to \neg \bot  \\
2 & & (\neg \varphi \to  \neg \bot)  \to ((\neg \varphi \to  \bot) \to \varphi) & \textsf{A3}[\varphi/p, \bot/q]\\
3 & & (\neg \varphi \to  \bot) \to \varphi & \textsf{MP} \ 1, 2\\
4 & & \neg \varphi \to \bot &  \Gamma \vdash \neg \varphi \to \bot \\
5 & & \varphi & \textsf{MP} \ 3, 4\\
\end{array}
$$
Steps 1 and 4 rely on two key observations:

1. $\Gamma \vdash \neg \varphi \to \bot$, which follows from the Deduction Theorem.
2. $\Gamma \vdash \neg \varphi \to \neg \bot$. Since $\Gamma, \neg \varphi \vdash \top$, and $\vdash \top \to \neg \neg \bot$, $\Gamma, \neg \varphi \vdash \neg \neg \top$. Since $\neg \neg \top$ is $\neg \bot$, we infer $\Gamma, \neg \varphi \vdash \neg \bot$. 

:::

## maximal consistency

::: {.definition}
A set of formulas $\Gamma$ is *maximal consistent* iff 

1. $\Gamma$ is consistent, and

2. for every formula $\varphi$, $\Gamma, \varphi$ is consistent *only if* $\varphi \in \Gamma$
:::




::: {.theorem}
Given a *maximal consistent* set of formulas $\Gamma$ and two formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$,
$$
\begin{array}{llll}
1. &\Gamma \vdash \varphi &  \Leftrightarrow & \varphi \in \Gamma\\
2. & \neg \varphi \in \Gamma & \Leftrightarrow & \varphi \notin \Gamma\\
3. & (\varphi \to \psi) \in \Gamma & \Leftrightarrow & \varphi \notin \Gamma \ \text{or} \ \psi \in \Gamma
\end{array}
$$
:::

---

::: {.proof}
Given a *maximal consistent* set $\Gamma$ and a formula $\varphi$:
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
 &\Gamma \vdash \varphi &  \Leftrightarrow & \varphi \in \Gamma\\
\end{array}
$$


($\Rightarrow$) Assume $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$. Suppose, for a reductio, that $\varphi \notin \Gamma$. By definition of *maximal consistency*, $\Gamma, \varphi$ is inconsistent. Since $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$, $\Gamma$ alone must be inconsistent. Contradiction.
<br/>
<br/>

($\Leftarrow$) If $\varphi \in \Gamma$, then there is a one-line derivation of $\varphi$ from $\Gamma$.

:::

---

::: {.proof}
Given a *maximal consistent* set $\Gamma$ and a formula $\varphi$:
$$
\begin{array}{llll}
 &\neg \varphi \in \Gamma &  \Leftrightarrow & \varphi \notin \Gamma\\
\end{array}
$$

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $\neg \varphi \in \Gamma$. By 1, $\Gamma \vdash \neg \varphi$. Since $\Gamma$ is consistent, $\Gamma \nvdash \varphi$, and, by 1 again, $\varphi \notin \Gamma$.

The crucial step is to note that $\vdash \neg \varphi \to (\varphi \to \bot)$ (4.7). So, if $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$, then, by two applications of \textsf{MP}, $\Gamma \vdash \bot$.
<br/>
<br/>

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\varphi \notin \Gamma$. By *maximal consistency*, $\Gamma, \varphi$ is inconsistent. Given 4.4. and 4.5. $\Gamma, \neg \neg \varphi$ is inconsistent. So, by 5.1., $\Gamma \vdash \neg \varphi$.

:::

---

::: {.proof}
Given a *maximal consistent* set $\Gamma$ and two formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$:
$$
\begin{array}{llll}
 &\varphi \to \psi \in \Gamma &  \Leftrightarrow & \varphi \notin \Gamma \ \text{or} \ \psi \in \Gamma\\
\end{array}
$$

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $\varphi \to \psi \in \Gamma$. Then $\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi$. We now argue that if $\varphi \in \Gamma$, then $\psi \in \Gamma$. If $\varphi \in \Gamma$, then $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ and $\Gamma \vdash \psi$. By 1 above, $\psi \in \Gamma$.
<br/>
<br/>

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\varphi \notin \Gamma$ or $\psi \in \Gamma$.

- If $\varphi \notin \Gamma$, then $\Gamma \vdash \neg \varphi$. Since $\Gamma \vdash \neg \varphi \to (\varphi \to \psi)$, we infer that $\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi$.

- If $\psi \in \Gamma$, then $\Gamma \vdash \psi$. Since $\Gamma \vdash \psi \to (\varphi \to \psi)$, we infer that $\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi$.

Notice that $\psi \to (\varphi \to \psi)$ is a substitution instance of axiom 1.
:::

# completeness {.divider}

::: {style="border: 2px solid #7f8c8d; background: #f8f9fa; padding: 0.5em 1em; border-radius: 6px; margin-top: 1.2em;"}
For all sets of formulas $\Gamma$ and formula $\varphi$, 

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \nvdash \varphi & \Rightarrow &\Gamma \not \models \varphi\\
\Gamma \models \varphi & \Rightarrow & \Gamma \vdash \varphi \\
\Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \textsf{consistent} & \Rightarrow & \Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \textsf{satisfiable} \\
\end{array}
$$

For all sets of formulas $\Gamma$,

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma  \ \textsf{consistent} & \Rightarrow & \Gamma \ \textsf{satisfiable} \\
\end{array}
$$
:::

## from consistency to satisfiability {.divider}

## the gap

On one side, a *syntactic* condition on a set of formulas $\Gamma$:

- $\Gamma$ is **consistent** iff $\bot$ is **not** derivable from $\Gamma$.

. . .

On the other side, a *semantic* condition on $\Gamma$:

- $\Gamma$ is **satisfiable** iff some valuation $V$ makes every formula in $\Gamma$ true.

. . .

We want to bridge the two:

$$\Gamma \ \text{consistent} \ \Longrightarrow \ \Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}.$$

## the plan 

Given a consistent set $\Gamma$, we will explain how to expand it into a *maximal consistent* set $\Gamma^+$.


<br/>
<br/>


::: {.r-stack style="justify-content:center; text-align:center;"}

::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index=1}
$$\begin{array}{clllc}
 \Gamma \ \text{consistent} & & & & \phantom{\Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}}\\
 \phantom{\Downarrow} & & & & \phantom{\Uparrow}\\
 \phantom{\Gamma^+ \ \text{maximal consistent}} & & \phantom{\Rightarrow} & & \phantom{\Gamma^+  \ \text{satisfiable}}\\
\end{array}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index=1}
$$\begin{array}{clllc}
 \Gamma \ \text{consistent} & & & & \phantom{\Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}}\\
 \Downarrow & & & & \phantom{\Uparrow}\\
 \Gamma^+ \ \text{maximal consistent} & & \phantom{\Rightarrow} & & \phantom{\Gamma^+  \ \text{satisfiable}}\\\\
\end{array}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index=2}
$$\begin{array}{clllc}
 \Gamma \ \text{consistent} & & & & \phantom{\Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}}\\
 \Downarrow & & & & \phantom{\Uparrow}\\
 \Gamma^+ \ \text{maximal consistent} & & \Rightarrow & & \Gamma^+  \ \text{satisfiable}\\
\end{array}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index=3}
$$\begin{array}{clllc}
 \Gamma \ \text{consistent} & & & & \Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}\\
 \Downarrow & & & & \Uparrow\\
 \Gamma^+ \text{maximal consistent} & & \Rightarrow & & \Gamma^+  \ \text{satisfiable}
\end{array}$$
:::

:::

## three arrows {.smaller}

1. from $\Gamma$ is consistent to $\Gamma^+$ is *maximal consistent*

::: {.theorem}
**Lindenbaum theorem**. Every *consistent* set $\Gamma$ is a subset of a *maximal consistent* set $\Gamma^+$.
:::

. . . 

2. from $\Gamma^+$ is *maximal consistent* to $\Gamma^+$ is *satisfiable*.

:::{.theorem}
**Henkin lemma**. Every *maximal consistent* set $\Sigma$ is satisfiable under the assignment
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
v(p) = 1 & \Leftrightarrow & p \in \Sigma
\end{array}
$$
:::

. . . 

3. from $\Gamma^+$ is *satisfiable* to $\Gamma$ is *satisfiable*.

::: {.theorem}
Every subset of a satisfiable set is satisfiable.
:::
